Description: implicit — point symbols camouflaged against aerial imagery
prompt: I have custom point icons on a MapLibre GL JS map over satellite/aerial imagery. Green icons vanish over vegetation and brown ones disappear over bare ground — they camouflage against whatever is behind them. How do I make the icons reliably stand out across all the different backgrounds in the imagery?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step-by-step recipe** that turns “green-over-grass / brown-over-soil” icons into **reliable, high-contrast symbols** on any satellite or aerial image.  
All the tricks come from the *MapLibre-Cartography* skill – halo/edge treatment, saturated fills, contact-shadows, SDF sprites, and layer ordering.

---

## 1. The core idea – “halo + saturated fill”

* **Why a halo works** – The halo is drawn *outside* the icon’s SDF shape, so it sits **between the icon and the photo** no matter what the photo’s hue is.  
* **Why a saturated fill works** – Imagery is usually low-saturation (desaturated greens, browns, greys). A bright, fully-saturated hue (amber, terracotta, cyan) stands out even when the background contains the same hue at a muted level.

**Rule of thumb for imagery basemaps**

| Property | Recommended value |
|----------|-------------------|
| `icon-color` (fill) | **Fully-saturated** earth-tone (e.g. `#ff8800` amber, `#e64a19` terracotta, `#00bcd4` cyan) |
| `icon-halo-color` | Dark semi-transparent: `rgba(0,0,0,0.75)` |
| `icon-halo-width` | 1.5 – 2.5 px (thin enough to look like an outline, thick enough to survive busy backgrounds) |
| `icon-opacity` | `1` (opaque – never semi-transparent over imagery) |

> **Tip:** If you already have a semantic colour (e.g. green for parks), keep the hue but **increase its chroma** (use a bright “lime” `#a8e600` instead of a muted `#6b8e23`). The halo will still guarantee contrast.

---

## 2. Turn your SVG icons into **SDF sprites** (so halos work)

Only **SDF (Signed Distance Field)** images can be given a halo via `icon-halo-*` paint properties. The conversion is cheap and works for any vector-style icon.

### 2.1 Prepare the SVG

1. **Make the shape a single solid path** (no fills that you want to keep transparent).  
2. **Add a 2-pixel padding** around the viewBox – the halo will be drawn into that space.  
3. **Optional:** bake a **contact-shadow** (a blurred ellipse under the icon) into the SVG. This gives the icon a “grounded” feel and further separates it from the photo.

```svg
<svg viewBox="-2 -2 36 36" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <!-- contact shadow -->
  <ellipse cx="16" cy="30" rx="12" ry="4"
           fill="rgba(0,0,0,0.3)" filter="url(#blur)"/>
  <defs>
    <filter id="blur"><feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="2"/></filter>
  </defs>

  <!-- the actual icon (solid path, no fill) -->
  <path d="M16 2 L22 12 L30 14 L24 22 L26 30 L16 26 L6 30 L8 22 L2 14 L10 12 Z"
        fill="currentColor"/>
</svg>
```

*`currentColor`* lets you recolor the icon later with `icon-color`.

### 2.2 Load the SVG as an SDF image

```js
// Helper: fetch an SVG, turn it into an Image, then add it as an SDF sprite
async function addSdfIcon(map, id, url) {
  const resp = await fetch(url);
  const svgText = await resp.text();

  // Turn the SVG string into a Blob → Image
  const blob = new Blob([svgText], {type: 'image/svg+xml'});
  const img = new Image();
  img.src = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
  await img.decode();               // wait for rasterisation

  // Add to the map – note the {sdf: true} flag
  map.addImage(id, img, { sdf: true, pixelRatio: 2 });
}

// Usage
addSdfIcon(map, 'park-icon', '/icons/park.svg');
addSdfIcon(map, 'farm-icon', '/icons/farm.svg');
```

> **Why `pixelRatio: 2`?** Most modern screens are Hi-DPI; a 2× rasterised sprite keeps the halo crisp at zoom-in.

---

## 3. Style the icon layer

```json
{
  "id": "custom-points",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "my-points",               // a GeoJSON or vector source
  "layout": {
    "icon-image": ["get", "icon_id"], // e.g. "park-icon" or "farm-icon"
    "icon-allow-overlap": true,
    "icon-ignore-placement": false,
    "icon-size": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
                  10, 0.6,
                  14, 1.0]               // optional size ramp
  },
  "paint": {
    // 1️⃣ Saturated fill – you can drive it per-feature if you need different hues
    "icon-color": [
      "match",
      ["get", "type"],
      "park", "#a8e600",          // bright lime
      "farm", "#ff8800",          // bright amber
      "#ffffff"                  // fallback (white)
    ],

    // 2️⃣ Dark semi-transparent halo – works on any background
    "icon-halo-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.75)",
    "icon-halo-width": 2,

    // 3️⃣ Optional extra contrast for very dense zoom levels
    "icon-opacity": ["step", ["zoom"], 0.9, 12, 1.0]
  }
}
```

### What each property does

| Paint property | Effect |
|----------------|--------|
| `icon-color` | Sets the **saturated fill**. Use a bright hue; you can also data-drive it (`match`, `case`, etc.). |
| `icon-halo-color` | Dark halo that *always* separates the icon from the photo. The `rgba(...,0.75)` gives a soft edge without a hard “sticker” look. |
| `icon-halo-width` | Thickness of the halo. 1.5 – 2.5 px is a sweet spot for 12-24 px icons. |
| `icon-allow-overlap` | Lets many points sit close together; the halo still protects each one. |
| `icon-size` | Optional size ramp – larger at higher zoom, but keep the halo width constant (it scales automatically). |
| `icon-opacity` | Keep the icon fully opaque; never set < 0.8 on imagery. |

---

## 4. Add a **contact-shadow** (optional but highly effective)

If you baked the shadow into the SVG (see step 2.1) you’re done.  
If you prefer to keep the SVG pure and add the shadow in the style, you can **stack a second symbol layer** that draws a blurred ellipse underneath the icon:

```json
{
  "id": "custom-points-shadow",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "my-points",
  "layout": {
    "icon-image": "shadow-ellipse",   // a tiny SDF circle sprite you add once
    "icon-allow-overlap": true,
    "icon-ignore-placement": true,
    "icon-size": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"], 10, 0.8, 14, 1.2],
    "icon-translate": [0, 6]          // push the shadow down a few pixels
  },
  "paint": {
    "icon-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.3)",
    "icon-halo-width": 0,
    "icon-opacity": 1
  }
}
```

Place this **below** the main icon layer (order matters – see § 5). The result is a subtle “ground-contact” ellipse that anchors the icon to the terrain and further separates it from bright rooftops or snow.

---

## 5. **Layer ordering** – keep icons under labels but above the imagery

```js
// 1️⃣ Add the raster imagery (satellite) – already in the base style
// 2️⃣ Add hillshade (if you have it) – optional
// 3️⃣ Add your custom point-shadow layer (if you use one)
map.addLayer(shadowLayer, firstSymbolId);   // before any label layer

// 4️⃣ Add the main icon layer
map.addLayer(iconLayer, firstSymbolId);    // same insertion point

// 5️⃣ (Optional) Add a *label* layer for the points, *after* the basemap's own labels
map.addLayer(labelLayer, null);            // topmost
```

`firstSymbolId` is the ID of the **first symbol layer** in the basemap style (usually the road-labels layer). Inserting before it guarantees **your icons sit under all basemap text**, so you never hide a city name.

```js
const firstSymbolId = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id;
map.addLayer(iconLayer, firstSymbolId);   // inject at the right spot
```

---

## 6. Accessibility check – contrast of *icon + halo*

WCAG 2.1 AA for large graphics (≥ 18 pt ≈ 24 px) requires **3:1** contrast; for smaller graphics **4.5:1**. The **combined color** of the icon edge (halo) against the background is what matters.

* Use a tool like **WebAIM Contrast Checker** and sample a few typical background pixels (e.g., bright soil `#cfa15a`, dark forest `#2b4a2b`, water `#4a6b8c`).  
* With `icon-color: #ff8800` and `icon-halo-color: rgba(0,0,0,0.75)`, the effective contrast is > 7:1 on all three samples – well within AA.

If you ever need a **different halo** (e.g., a light halo for a dark-themed map), keep the same **opacity** (`0.75`) and increase the width so the contrast stays high.

Description: anti-pattern — reducing road opacity to calm bright roads on imagery
prompt: I dropped my OSM Bright vector road layers on top of satellite imagery and the bright orange/yellow roads look garish and dominate the map. My instinct is to lower their opacity so the imagery shows through. Is that the right fix?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  
**No – lowering the opacity of the OSM Bright road layers is the wrong fix.**  
A semi-transparent orange/yellow line lets the busy photographic background bleed through, which makes the roads look fuzzy, flat and still visually dominant. The cartographic-correct solution is to **re-palette the roads for an imagery basemap**:

1. **Desaturate the colors** (move them toward neutral greys).  
2. **Keep the roads opaque** (no `fill-opacity` or `line-opacity`).  
3. **Retain hierarchy with width and value**, not hue.  
4. **Add a darker casing** that contains the fill.  
5. **Optionally interpolate the colour/brightness by zoom** so low-zoom roads stay subtle.

Below is a step-by-step recipe, plus a ready-to-paste style snippet that you can drop into a MapLibre GL JS style that already contains a satellite raster source.

---

## 1️⃣ Why opacity isn’t the answer

| Problem | What happens when you lower opacity? |
|---------|---------------------------------------|
| **Contrast loss** | The road line blends with the underlying texture, making it hard to read at any zoom. |
| **Colour dominance** | The orange/yellow hue is still the most saturated element on the map, so it still “shouts” even when translucent. |
| **Visual hierarchy collapse** | Semi-transparent lines look like a faint overlay rather than a reference layer; they no longer convey the intended road-type hierarchy. |
| **Accessibility** | WCAG contrast ratios are calculated on the *combined* colour (road + background). A 30 %-transparent orange on a bright field can drop well below the 4.5:1 minimum for normal text-size labels that sit on the same road line. |

The cartographic principle is **“the reference layer should be visually subordinate to the subject layer.”** In an imagery map the *subject* is the photograph; the *reference* (roads) must be **muted, crisp, and opaque** so the viewer can still read the underlying terrain.

---

## 2️⃣ Re-palette the roads for imagery

### 2.1 Choose a neutral colour palette

| Road class | Typical OSM Bright colour | Recommended imagery colour |
|------------|---------------------------|----------------------------|
| Motorway / primary | `#f90` (bright orange) | `#4a4a4a` (mid-grey) |
| Trunk / secondary | `#fd4` (yellow-orange) | `#5e5e5e` (slightly lighter grey) |
| Tertiary / residential | `#b06010` (brown-orange) | `#777777` (light-grey) |
| Service / footway | `#c0c0c0` (light grey) | keep as `#c0c0c0` (no change) |

> **Tip:** Keep the hue *neutral* (no strong reds, blues, or greens). Neutral greys let the underlying colours of the imagery show through without competition.

### 2.2 Keep the roads **opaque**

```json
{
  "id": "road-fill",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "road",
  "filter": ["!=", ["get", "class"], "path"],   // example filter
  "paint": {
    "line-color": [
      "match",
      ["get", "class"],
      "motorway", "#4a4a4a",
      "trunk",    "#5e5e5e",
      "primary",  "#5e5e5e",
      "secondary","#777777",
      "tertiary", "#777777",
      "#c0c0c0"   // default for minor roads
    ],
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],
      ["zoom"],
      5, 0.5,
      10, 2,
      14, 6,
      18, 12
    ],
    "line-opacity": 1.0   // **explicitly opaque**
  }
}
```

### 2.3 Add a darker *casing* that contains the fill

```json
{
  "id": "road-casing",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "road",
  "filter": ["!=", ["get", "class"], "path"],
  "paint": {
    "line-color": [
      "match",
      ["get", "class"],
      "motorway", "#2b2b2b",
      "trunk",    "#3a3a3a",
      "primary",  "#3a3a3a",
      "secondary","#4f4f4f",
      "tertiary", "#4f4f4f",
      "#999999"
    ],
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],
      ["zoom"],
      5, 1,
      10, 3,
      14, 8,
      18, 14
    ],
    "line-opacity": 1.0
  }
}
```

**Why a darker casing?**  
A *knock-out* (darker than the fill) creates a crisp edge that separates the road from the imagery, especially on bright fields or rooftops. It also preserves the visual hierarchy without needing a saturated hue.

### 2.4 Interpolate colour/brightness by zoom (optional)

At low zoom you only see a few major roads; a slightly darker casing prevents them from looking too heavy. As you zoom in, lighten the casing so the road network doesn’t become a black-ink blob.

```json
{
  "id": "road-casing-zoom",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "road",
  "filter": ["!=", ["get", "class"], "path"],
  "paint": {
    "line-color": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],
      ["zoom"],
      5, "#2b2b2b",   // very dark at far-zoom
      10, "#3a3a3a",
      14, "#4f4f4f",
      18, "#5e5e5e"   // lighter at close-up
    ],
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],
      ["zoom"],
      5, 1,
      10, 3,
      14, 8,
      18, 14
    ]
  }
}
```

---

## 3️⃣ Layer ordering – make sure the roads stay **under** the basemap labels

1. **Raster imagery** (satellite) – bottommost raster source.  
2. **Hillshade** (if you have it).  
3. **Terrain fills** (land, water, parks).  
4. **Road casing** (drawn *before* the fill).  
5. **Road fill** (drawn *after* the casing).  
6. **Other vector layers** (boundaries, water lines, etc.).  
7. **Basemap symbol layers** (place-labels, road-labels).  
8. **Your custom symbols/labels** (if any).

In code, when you add your own road layers at runtime:

```js
// Find the first symbol layer in the existing style
const firstSymbolId = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id;

// Insert road casing below the first symbol layer
map.addLayer(roadCasingLayer, firstSymbolId);

// Insert road fill *above* the casing but still below the symbols
map.addLayer(roadFillLayer, firstSymbolId);
```

---

## 4️⃣ Fine-tuning for readability on imagery

| Property | Recommended value for imagery | Reason |
|----------|------------------------------|--------|
| `line-width` | Use the same width ramp as you would on a vector basemap, but **do not** boost it to compensate for the lack of colour contrast. | Width already encodes hierarchy. |
| `line-dasharray` | Avoid heavy dashes on major roads; use solid lines. Light dashes are okay for footpaths. | Dashes add visual noise on a busy photo. |
| `line-gap-width` | If you need a “double-line” look (e.g., for motorways), use `line-gap-width` **instead of** a second colour layer. | Keeps the road a single opaque element, preserving crispness. |
| `line-blur` | Keep at `0` (no blur). | Blur softens the edge and makes the road look like a shadow rather than a reference line. |
| `line-cap` / `line-join` | `"round"` for smooth curves, `"butt"` for straight segments. | Consistency with most vector basemap styles. |

---

## 5️⃣ Accessibility check

1. **Contrast** – Use a tool (WebAIM, Stark, or the built-in MapLibre style validator) to verify that the *combined* colour of road fill + casing meets **4.5:1** against the *average* background of your imagery.  
   - A mid-grey fill (`#777777`) with a dark casing (`#4f4f4f`) on typical satellite imagery usually lands around **5–6:1**.  
2. **Size** – Ensure the smallest road line width at the lowest zoom is at least **0.5 px** (rendered as a crisp line) and that labels attached to those roads have a minimum `text-size` of **10 px**.  
3. **Non-colour cues** – If you need to differentiate road classes for colour-blind users, add a subtle pattern (e.g., `line-dasharray`) or a slight width difference, not just hue.

---
